title: Ephemeral network saturation and scheduler fairness observations
content:
High level summary:

This document captures on-call notes and a preliminary incident review for the cluster-wide performance degradation observed 2024-11-07 03:10-03:55 UTC. Symptoms were elevated pod start latencies, a spike in scheduling pending pods, and a correlated increase in CNI retransmits/ARP timeouts on a subset of worker pools. We observed node-level memory pressure on the same timeframe on ~18% of nodes in the eu-west-1-gpu pool.

Impact:
- ~420 pods experienced Start->Running delays >120s (mostly short-lived batch jobs and autoscaler-created workers).
- Affected services: batch-transform, realtime-preproc (best-effort), and some canary runners.
- No customer-facing production API degradation (hosted inference frontends served from separate pools), but internal job queues backed up causing increased end-to-end batch latency.

Initial detection and alerting:
- Pager triggered from scheduler_alerts: PendingPodsHigh (threshold 200 pending in cluster) at 2024-11-07T03:12:06Z.
- SRE on-call (Avery) began triage at 03:13. Linked alert IDs: alert-9004, prometheus-rule-PendingPodsHigh-eu.
- We also received network errors from node-exporter logs indicating repeated CNI flapping on nic0 interface on nodes with index suffix -gpu-1xx.

Timeline (approx):
- 03:10 UTC: Autoscaler triggers scale-up; kube-scheduler backlog increases.
- 03:11 UTC: Multiple nodes in eu-west-1-gpu report kernel logs: "neigh: arp_cache overflow" and repeated "NETDEV WATCHDOG: eth0: transmit queue timeout" on nodes gpu-114, gpu-128, gpu-130.
- 03:15 UTC: kube-proxy conntrack table grows by 40% on affected nodes; CNI agent restarts observed (weave-daemonset respawned pods).
- 03:20 UTC: Manual cordon of gpu-114 and gpu-128 to stop new pods scheduling while we investigate.
- 03:28 UTC: We applied temporary sysctl bump for net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh3 on affected nodes from 1024 -> 8192 (to reduce ARP cache eviction pressure).
- 03:32 UTC: Observed slow recovery in packet drops but additional nodes (gpu-130, gpu-133) started showing similar symptoms; we began rolling small kernel parameter changes cluster-wide as mitigation.
- 03:46 UTC: Autoscaler spike subsided; pending pods count returned to normal by 03:55 UTC.

Key observations and hypotheses:
1) Memory- and socket-related pressure on nodes coincided with high churn from scale-up (many short-lived pods). The kernel neigh/ARP cache overflow messages imply many ephemeral IPs in the ARP table due to rapid pod churn and CNI re-allocations.
2) CNI datapath (weave) restarted on several nodes. Restarting CNI agents leads to transient packet loss and ephemeral connection resets which amplify pod start failures and kubelet retries.
3) Conntrack table growth combined with high ephemeral port usage contributed to NAT translation exhaustion for an internal control plane communication path (kubelet -> kube-apiserver), causing longer API retries and scheduling delays.
4) Scheduler fairness: default scheduler scored nodes with higher free allocatable resources as preferred; however, when some nodes experienced CNI instability, the scheduler still targeted them, causing pods to bounce. We saw repeated scheduling attempts for the same pod id across nodes.

Evidence snippets (sanitized):
- kernel log excerpt (gpu-128):
  Nov  7 03:11:02 gpu-128 kernel: neigh: arp_cache overflow, dropping neighbour 10.2.45.67 on dev eth0
  Nov  7 03:11:15 gpu-128 kernel: NETDEV WATCHDOG: eth0: transmit queue timeout

- kubelet logs (pod start failure):
  E1107 03:12:51.123 kubelet.go:218] Failed to create pod sandbox: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to setup network for sandbox "...": timeout waiting for CNI plugin ready

- conntrack stats (affected node, sampled):
  conntrack entries: 91234 -> high watermark ~128k during spike (default max 65536)

Mitigations applied during incident (short-term):
- Cordoned two most-affected nodes to stop scheduling while we recovered.
- Incremented net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh3 from 1024 to 8192 on affected nodes to reduce ARP churn-induced evictions.
- Increased conntrack max (net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max) from 65536 to 262144 on the fly using sysctl for the eu-west-1-gpu pool.
- Temporarily allowed kube-scheduler to prefer nodes with longer uptime via a soft taint preference: added "sre/avoid-recent-cni-restart" as a NodeAffinity soft rule on critical batch pods via a quick mutating admission override for 30m.
- Restarted weave-daemonset pods sequentially with 15s delay to avoid simultaneous CNI restarts.

Post-incident root cause analysis (preliminary):
- Primary driver: ephemeral network state saturation (ARP/neigh overflow + conntrack exhaustion) caused by a combination of aggressive autoscaler churn and a previously undetected weave datapath memory leak on older kernel versions present in a subset of GPU nodes.
- Secondary factors: scheduler continued to schedule onto nodes with degraded datapath because node readiness probes were still passing and the kubelet didn't mark the node NotReady until later.
- Concurrency of CNI restarts made the problem self-amplifying: when multiple nodes restart CNI, control-plane retries increase, leading to further churn.

Runbook gaps discovered:
- No automated knob in autoscaler to detect network saturation signals (we rely on CPU/memory metrics but not kernel-level netstat/conntrack indications).
- Runbooks for conntrack scaling are present but not linked in the alert workflow; on-call had to search Confluence mid-incident.
- We lack a lightweight node-level readiness signal that accounts for CNI datapath health (we currently rely on kubelet network-plugin readiness but it often reports healthy until a hard failure).

Immediate follow-ups / action items (owners and ETA):
- infra/kernel: schedule kernel upgrade for eu-west-1-gpu pool to include upstream fixes for weave-related memory smoothing (owner: Rahul Desai, ETA: 2024-11-29).
- sre/automation: add conntrack and arp/neigh saturation detectors to the autoscaler decision pipeline and create alerts (owner: Avery Chen, ETA: 2024-11-15).
- runbooks: add a dedicated CNI-saturation response section to the SRE runbook and link it to PendingPodsHigh alert (owner: Nina Ortiz, ETA: 2024-11-13).
- scheduler config: evaluate soft taints/affinities for nodes recently restarted or with CNI restarts; propose a scheduler score tweak to deprioritize nodes with CNI restart count > 1 in the last 10m (owner: Maya Thompson, ETA: 2024-11-20).
- monitoring: create Grafana dashboard panels for neigh/arp table utilization, conntrack high-water marks, and weave agent restart counts per node (owner: infra-observability, ETA: 2024-11-14).

Suggested durable mitigations (discussion items):
- Introduce a dedicated CNI-health probe that exposes datapath drop rate and restart count to Node condition. If datapath_drop_rate > X or restart_count > Y => set node condition CNIDegraded and have scheduler deprioritize.
- Autoscaler: add a safeguard to limit scale-up rate when network path metrics exceed thresholds to avoid amplifying churn.
- Conntrack tuning: persist higher nf_conntrack_max for the GPU pools and ensure nodes reserved for high-churn workloads have larger headroom.
- Consider moving short-lived batch workers to a separate node pool with different CNI parameters and lower density to reduce ARP churn.

Playbook snippets to include in runbook (commands used during incident):
- Check conntrack usage: sudo conntrack -L | wc -l; sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max
- Increase conntrack on-the-fly: sudo sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=262144
- Inspect kernel neigh stats: cat /proc/net/arp; ip -s neigh show dev eth0
- Soft cordon node: kubectl cordon gpu-128
- Drain safely (if needed): kubectl drain gpu-128 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force
- Sequential CNI restart: for n in $(kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l name=weave-net -o name); do kubectl delete $n; sleep 15; done

Unresolved questions (to investigate):
- Was there an underlying external network event (switch port flaps) that coincided, or is this purely local to node kernel/CNI? We already asked infra networking for switch port logs; awaiting their feed.
- Did any of the affected nodes have different VM host configurations (older kernel, different AMI) compared to the rest of the pool?
- Can we reproduce locally by generating similar churn (rapid pod creation/deletion) on a test pool with older kernels and measuring neigh/conntrack behavior?

Notes for postmortem (if elevated):
- Include sequence diagrams of autoscaler actions, CNI restarts, and scheduler reschedules to show amplification loop.
- Quantify customer impact in terms of delayed batch jobs for the last 24h and cost overhead due to retries.

Appendix (investigation artifacts):
- prometheus query samples used: sum by (instance) (conntrack_count{job="node-exporter"})
- heuristics used to detect CNI restarts: increase in kube-system pod restarts for weave-net over 5m window > 2
- related jira: JIRA-OPS-4312 (incident ticket), JIRA-DEV-5820 (weave memory leak investigation)

If anything missing or unclear, tag and add notes inline. This is a working doc; will convert to a formal incident review if scope and customer impact warrant escalation.
